bp: A search system often has to find the right document without reading every document in full at answer time. One practical shortcut is to store a shorter version of each document, then search over those summaries. That saves space and may make the important parts easier to compare with a user's query. But a summary written to sound fluent is not automatically a good search object. It may omit the exact clue that would make the document retrievable, or it may use wording that no longer matches the way the retriever learned to compare queries and full documents. ReSuMe serves this pressure point. It treats summarization and retrieval as two parts of one machine: the summarizer must produce document shortcuts that help search, and the retriever must learn how to search those shortcuts. The goal is not merely nicer summaries, but summaries that preserve the evidence a dense retriever needs to rank documents.
wh: The hard part is that the retriever and the summarizer can silently disagree about what a document is. A dense retriever is a model that turns a query and each document into comparable numeric descriptions, then ranks documents by closeness. If it was trained on full documents, its sense of closeness is shaped by full-document wording, length, and detail. At inference time, ReSuMe's setting asks that retriever to operate on synthetic summaries instead. That creates a distribution shift, meaning the material seen at use time has a different shape from the material seen during training. A readable summary can still be a bad retrieval target if it drops rare facts, changes wording, or compresses several ideas into vague language. The central tension is compression versus findability: summaries should be short, but search needs the specific traces that distinguish one relevant document from many plausible neighbors.
naive: A smart beginner would build the system in two separate steps. First, train or choose a summarizer that writes high-quality document summaries. Second, give those summaries to an existing dense retriever and expect search to become cheaper and perhaps cleaner. This fails because linguistic quality and retrieval usefulness are not the same objective. A summary can be grammatical, concise, and faithful while still removing the phrase, entity, or detail that would match a query. The retriever also has no reason to understand the summarizer's preferred style if it learned from full documents. The pipeline breaks at the boundary between the two models: each component looks reasonable alone, but the pair is not trained to agree.
ap: ReSuMe's core idea is to make the summarizer and retriever adapt to each other instead of freezing one side and hoping the other side fits. The language model is trained to generate summaries whose value is judged by retrieval relevance, not by wording quality alone. At the same time, the retrieval model is updated on those generated summaries so it learns the new kind of document representation it will actually face. The process alternates: improve the summarizer using feedback from retrieval, then improve the retriever using the summaries the current summarizer produces. In concrete terms, the paper turns summarization into a search-serving action. A summary is good when it helps a relevant document rise in the ranked list for the right query. The repeated back-and-forth is meant to reduce the gap between full-document training and summary-based inference.
mech: The mechanism begins with documents, queries, and a dense retrieval system such as Contriever. The summarizer first produces synthetic summaries of documents. These summaries are not treated as final products judged only by human-like readability. They become the objects that the retriever must search. Next, the language model behind the summarizer is fine-tuned with Group Relative Policy Optimization, a reinforcement-learning procedure where several candidate outputs can be compared as a group and the model is pushed toward outputs that receive better reward. Here the reward is tied to retrieval relevance: a summary is favored when using it helps the retriever place the right document higher. Then the retriever is updated on the generated summaries using contrastive learning, which means learning by pulling matching query-summary pairs closer and pushing mismatched pairs farther apart in the retriever's comparison space. After that retriever update, the summarizer faces a changed search partner, so the process can repeat. Each phase changes the environment for the other phase: better summaries give the retriever cleaner training material, and a retriever adapted to those summaries gives more meaningful feedback to the summarizer. The output is a pair of models, one producing retrieval-oriented summaries and one searching those summaries more effectively.
math: The main mathematical ideas are scoring, comparison, and alternating optimization. Scoring means deciding what counts as a better summary. ReSuMe does not make fluency the only score; it uses retrieval relevance, so the score asks whether the summary helps a query find the correct document. Comparison appears inside dense retrieval: query text and summary text are converted into numeric descriptions, and closeness between those descriptions becomes the basis for ranking. This is a useful compression of meaning, but it is also lossy: many document details must be squeezed into a limited numeric form, so the system must learn which details matter for search. Reinforcement learning enters as trial-and-feedback learning for the summarizer. The model tries different summary wordings and is rewarded when they improve retrieval behavior. Group Relative Policy Optimization, as named in the abstract, adds relative comparison among candidate outputs rather than judging each output in isolation. Contrastive learning is the retriever's matching math: make true query-summary pairs closer than false pairs. The alternating structure matters because each side changes the data seen by the other. The tradeoff is compression versus discriminative detail, with training pressure used to keep shortened text searchable.
dots: This paper sits in the repo's information-retrieval and search family because its basic object is a ranked list: from a large document collection, show the documents most likely to answer a query. It also neighbors the retrieval-augmented generation family, where many papers ask whether the information fed into a language model is actually useful rather than merely related. ReSuMe is upstream of that concern: before an answer model reasons over retrieved material, the retriever must first find the right material from compact document surrogates. The paper connects to ranking, similarity, language models, and optimization. Ranking decides which documents get surfaced; similarity decides what counts as close enough; the language model writes the searchable summaries; optimization repeatedly changes model behavior to reduce retrieval errors. Compared with RAG papers that prune evidence chains, handle conflicts, or decide when to retrieve, ReSuMe focuses on making the document representation itself search-ready.
ww: The method should work when the main failure is mismatch between the form of stored documents and the form the retriever learned to search. If summaries are created independently, the retriever sees shortened text with different wording and missing detail. ReSuMe attacks that mismatch from both directions. The summarizer receives a reward tied to whether its output helps retrieval, so it has pressure to keep query-relevant identifiers, distinctions, and phrases rather than only writing a pleasant abstract. The retriever then learns from the summaries it will actually compare against queries, so its notion of closeness adapts to compressed document text. Alternation is important because one fixed update is unlikely to solve the problem: as summaries become more retrieval-oriented, the best retriever behavior changes; as the retriever adapts, the feedback given to the summarizer becomes more aligned with the final use case. The abstract's reported gains on MS-MARCO with Contriever suggest that reducing this train-use gap can improve ranked retrieval rather than merely producing shorter documents.
po: The payoff is a document summarizer and retriever that are trained as a cooperative pair. Grounded in the abstract, ReSuMe improves retrieval while also producing summaries optimized for retrieval tasks. In experiments with Contriever on MS-MARCO, the paper reports consistent improvements of 13.2 percent in MRR@10, which measures whether highly ranked results put the right answer near the top, and 6.7 percent in Recall@100, which measures whether relevant material appears within the first hundred results. The practical capability is efficient search over synthetic summaries without paying the full penalty of using a retriever trained only on full documents.
limits: The abstract supports the general claim but leaves important assumptions open. The approach assumes retrieval relevance is a sufficient training signal for summaries; it may not capture every human need, such as completeness, citation usefulness, or faithful preservation of nuance. It also assumes alternating fine-tuning remains stable and worth its cost for a given deployment. The empirical evidence named in the abstract uses Contriever and MS-MARCO, so the model-agnostic claim still depends on other retrievers, datasets, domains, and summary lengths behaving similarly. The method reduces the gap between full documents and synthetic summaries, but the abstract does not prove that no important facts are lost during summarization.
